title: SpaceX Falcon 9 Rocket Stage on Track to Crash Into the Moon on August 5
excerpt: A spent upper stage from a 2025 lunar mission will slam into the surface near Einstein crater at 5,400 mph, creating a dust plume that astronomers worldwide plan to observe.
body:
• A spent SpaceX Falcon 9 upper stage is projected to crash into the Moon near Einstein crater on August 5 at 2:44 a.m. EDT (6:44 UTC), traveling at roughly 5,400 mph.
  • The 39-foot-long, 4,000-kilogram hollow shell has been drifting in a high orbit since January 2025, when it launched two commercial lunar landers.
  • A team of 23 astronomers has called on the scientific community to observe the impact, which could produce a visible dust plume and a crater 20 to 30 meters wide.
  • The event highlights the growing problem of uncontrolled space debris near the Moon as multiple nations, including India, plan future lunar missions.

A Rocket Left to Drift

On January 15, 2025, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launched from Florida carrying two commercial lunar landers — Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost and Japanese firm ispace's Hakuto-R2. Blue Ghost successfully touched down on the Moon in March 2025 and operated for two weeks, capturing the first solar eclipse from the lunar surface. Hakuto-R2's Resilience lander was less fortunate, crash-landing in June 2025.

The Falcon 9's upper stage, meanwhile, was supposed to burn up on reentry into Earth's atmosphere. That did not happen. Instead, the spent booster entered a high elliptical orbit around Earth with a period of about 26 days, taking it roughly as far out as the Moon. It has been drifting ever since, catalogued as object 2025-010D.

Independent astronomer Bill Gray, developer of the widely used Project Pluto tracking software, was the first to calculate that the object would eventually hit the Moon. Based on over 1,000 observations gathered by asteroid surveys and telescopes, Gray projects the impact will occur near Einstein crater on the boundary between the lunar near side and far side.

What the Impact Will Look Like

The upper stage measures about 39 feet long and 13 feet wide, roughly the size of a semi-truck trailer, with a mass of approximately 4,000 kilograms. It will strike the Moon at about 5,400 mph — seven times the speed of sound.

In a paper posted to the preprint server arXiv, 23 astronomers modeled what will happen on impact. Because the rocket is a hollow metal shell rather than a solid asteroid, it will crush on contact rather than penetrate deeply. The collision is expected to blast open a new crater roughly 20 to 30 meters wide and launch a cloud of lunar dust several kilometers above the surface.

"Potential observables from this event include the flash at the time of impact and the ejecta plume."

— arXiv preprint by 23 astronomers

The dust cloud is exactly what researchers are hoping to study. The impact will occur when the Moon is in waning gibbous phase, visible in pre-dawn skies from the Americas. Ground-based telescopes and orbital spacecraft, including NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, may be positioned to capture the event.

The Growing Debris Problem Beyond Earth Orbit

While space debris in low Earth orbit is a well-documented concern, the Falcon 9 impact highlights an emerging challenge closer to the Moon. As NASA's Artemis program, China's Chang'e missions, and India's Chandrayaan-4 lunar sample return mission ramp up activity around the Moon, the risk of uncontrolled hardware colliding with the surface — or with other spacecraft — is growing.

Gray notes that objects at lunar distances are poorly tracked compared to low-orbit debris. The US Space Force's radar systems, which monitor thousands of objects in low Earth orbit, struggle at lunar range where radar signals are about 25.6 million times fainter.

"The motion of space junk is mostly quite predictable; it simply moves under the influence of the gravity of the Earth, Moon, Sun, and planets," Gray wrote. But solar radiation pressure — the subtle push of sunlight on a tumbling object — adds up unpredictably over months, making long-range forecasts difficult.

This is not the first time a rocket stage has struck the Moon. A Chinese Long March 5B upper stage hit the far side in March 2022, creating a double crater discovered by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. But the August 5 event will be the first with enough advance warning for astronomers to attempt real-time observation.
nri_angle: The uncontrolled lunar impact underscores the growing space debris problem as India's ISRO prepares its own Chandrayaan-4 lunar sample return mission.
